Guidance for 3 year accreditation practical exercises for Oil Spill Response Organisations
This guidance explains what is expected during practical exercises for accreditation and re-accreditation under the UK National Standard for Marine Oil Spill Response Organisations. It should be read alongside Appendix 4 of the standard.
What is the purpose of the practical exercise?
The practical exercise is used to demonstrate and validate an Oil Spill Response Organisations (OSRO) operational capability to the Accrediting Body and, ultimately, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA).
Unlike routine training exercises, it is not primarily intended as an opportunity to coach or train staff.
What should be demonstrated during the exercise?
OSROs should discuss exercise requirements with the Accrediting Body before the exercise takes place.
In addition to demonstrating the ability to respond to a hydrocarbon spill, the exercise should show how the organisation manages the wider response.
Including:
- command and control arrangements
- communication with clients and stakeholders
- communication methods, such as radio and digital systems
- toolbox talks, site set-up and demobilisation
- decontamination procedures
- risk assessments, safety management and first aid arrangements
- record keeping and logging
Where clients or stakeholders are role-played, the approach should be agreed with the Accrediting Body in advance.
The exercise should demonstrate the full response process, from activation through to demobilisation. Simulated or notional elements, such as assumed permissions, equipment availability or phone calls, should be kept to a minimum.
How should exercises be managed for organisations operating across multiple regions?
OSROs with a wide geographical area of operation should use a realistic selection of responders during the exercise.
For example, if an exercise is held in the north of Scotland, most responders should normally be located within the agreed 6 hour response time, or any contracted response radius for that area. Any exceptions should be agreed with the Accrediting Body before the exercise.
Organisations providing multi-regional coverage should also aim to vary exercise locations over time. For example, if an exercise takes place in south-west England during the initial accreditation period, the re-accreditation exercise would not normally be expected to take place in the same region.
What if an organisation holds accreditation for multiple modules?
OSROs accredited for multiple response modules should discuss exercise arrangements with the Accrediting Body in advance.
Where possible, opportunities should be provided throughout the 3 year accreditation period for the Accrediting Body to observe different response modules.
For example, it may not be practical to demonstrate offshore, shoreline and enclosed harbour response capabilities within a single exercise. In these situations, one exercise could demonstrate shoreline and enclosed harbour capabilities, while an offshore deployment is observed separately during the accreditation period.
Organisations accredited for multiple modules are not normally expected to demonstrate the same module during consecutive accreditation assessments. For example, an organisation that demonstrated shoreline response capability during initial accreditation should not rely solely on a shoreline exercise for re-accreditation three years later.
What happens if the required standard is not met?
The process is set out in Appendix 4 of the standard.
The action required will depend on the nature and severity of any deficiencies identified.
Serious shortcomings, such as unsafe working practices or incorrect use of equipment, are likely to require a repeat exercise. Minor issues may be addressed within an agreed timescale between the OSRO, the Accrediting Body and the MCA.
Can exercises completed during the 3 year accreditation period contribute to re-accreditation?
Yes. OSROs are encouraged to invite Accrediting Bodies to observe routine exercises, particularly where these demonstrate capabilities within modules that have not been assessed recently.
This may help reduce the scope and complexity of the formal 3 year re-accreditation exercise.
If an organisation wishes to complete its re-accreditation exercise before the current 3-year accreditation period expires and start a new accreditation cycle, it should agree arrangements directly with its Accrediting Body.
